title: Architecture and Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Guidance
author: Elena Park
body:
Overview
This page consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It is intended as the canonical reference for new services, major refactors, and ADRs that affect run-time behaviour or operational guarantees.

Scope
- Applies to all hosted, dedicated, and private control plane services and runtime components.
- Includes public REST/SDK surfaces, internal RPCs, Runtime kernels, orchestration, and monitoring.
- Does not replace language- or team-specific style guides but adds company-wide constraints and operational requirements.

1) API Standards
Goal: predictable, stable APIs that are discoverable, versioned, and observable.
Key rules:
- OpenAPI 3.x spec required for every public or partner-facing endpoint. Specs must live in the service repo under /api/openapi.yaml and be validated in CI.
- Semantic versioning for public APIs. Base path contains major version: /v1/, /v2/. Minor/patch changes should be behind feature flags or new endpoints.
- Authentication: Bearer tokens (OAuth2 or service tokens). Use scopes for fine-grained permissions. All calls must validate token expiry and scope.
- Rate limiting: 429 responses for quota breaches. API should return X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and Retry-After when applicable. Default hosted limit: 100 req/s per API key (product-managed tiers override).
- Error model (JSON): always return {"error": {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional}}. Standard codes: invalid_request, unauthorized, forbidden, not_found, rate_limit_exceeded, validation_error, server_error. Use 4xx for client issues, 5xx for server.
- Idempotency: for non-idempotent operations (e.g. POST /generations), support Idempotency-Key header. Servers should store request hash for 24 hours.
- Pagination: cursor-based. Use { items: [...], next_cursor: string | null, page_size: int }. Avoid offset pagination for large collections.
- Streaming: use chunked HTTP responses with well-defined event JSON payloads and final status chunk. Document expected stream markers in OpenAPI.
- API stability: Deprecation header X-Deprecated-Until + deprecation advisories 90 days before removal for public APIs.

Example request/response snippet (cursor pagination):
Request: GET /v1/models?limit=50
Response: {
  "items": [{"model_id": "redwood-7b", "status": "available"}],
  "next_cursor": "eyJvZmZzZXQiOjUwLCJpZCI6bnVsbH0="
}

2) Coding Standards
Goal: readable, testable, and performant code across stacks.
Cross-team rules:
- Languages: Go for core runtime and infra services; Python for experiments/evals and data tooling; TypeScript for Console and SDKs. Teams may propose new languages with an ADR.
- Formatting & linting: gofmt + golangci-lint; black + ruff (Python); prettier + eslint (TypeScript). CI must fail on formatter/linter issues.
- Testing: unit tests required. Services must include integration tests that run in CI (mocked infra allowed). Performance-sensitive code must include microbenchmarks.
- PR guidance: keep PRs focused (recommended < 500 lines), include release notes for public-facing changes, list owners, and link ADRs where relevant.
- Feature flags: all behavioural changes must be behind flags for staged rollouts. Use the central flags service; document flags in the repo README.

3) Infrastructure Standards
Goal: reproducible, auditable infra with minimal blast radius.
Standards:
- IaC: Terraform v1.4+ modules. Modules published to internal registry. Remote state stored in S3 with DynamoDB locking for AWS; equivalent constructs for other clouds.
- Secrets: Vault for runtime secrets; KMS-wrapped secrets for long-term storage. No plaintext secrets in repos or CI logs.
- Networking: VPCs with least-privilege security groups. All customer-facing endpoints must support TLS1.2+. Private deployments must support customer-managed network overlays.
- CI/CD: pipelines must include terraform plan apply gates, security scans (SNYK/Trivy), and an automated canary deployment workflow for runtime services.
- Observability hooks: every service must register dashboards (Grafana), SLO pages, and alerts on the central alerting team.

4) Model-serving Standards
Goal: consistent, safe, and cost-predictable model serving across deployments.
Requirements:
- Model catalog: each model entry must include model_id, architecture, quantization profile, expected memory and throughput, quality metrics (per-eval), and owner. Catalog stored in repo /models/catalog.yaml.
- Versioning: immutable model artifacts. Model IDs include semantic model version (e.g., redwood-7b-v1.2). Runtime uses explicit model pins; default aliasing (e.g., latest-stable) allowed but must be opt-in.
- Rollout policy (canary):
  1) Canary at 1% traffic for 24h. Collect metric deltas vs baseline.
  2) If no regression, ramp to 10% for 48h.
  3) Ramp to 50% for 24h, then 100% if all checks pass.
Rollback criteria (any triggers rollback):
  - Absolute quality metric regression > 2.0% on production eval set.
  - End-to-end p95 latency increase > 20% vs baseline.
  - Error rate increase > 0.5 percentage points.
- Quantization & accuracy: recommended quantization profiles live in /quantization-profiles. For customer-facing models, require an explicit quality validation suite that runs before publishing a quantized variant.
- Caching & batching:
  - KV cache: LRU with TTL 24h (default), size per model documented in catalog.
  - Batching: runtime supports dynamic batching window (10-50ms). Default max batch sizes by GPU class: A100: 64, H100: 96, T4: 16. These values must be validated in benchmarking suite.
- Safety & filtering: use the central content-filtering library. Safety policies must be applied uniformly across Hosted and Dedicated.

5) Observability Standards
Goal: fast detection and root-cause analysis through consistent metrics, logs, and traces.
Metrics:
- Mandatory metrics (names): request_count, request_error_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), inference_batch_size, kv_cache_hit_rate, model_load_time_seconds. Expose model-specific labels: model_id, model_version, region, deployment_tier.
- SLOs should be derived from these metrics and published to SLO pages.
Tracing & Logs:
- Correlation: every incoming request must carry a correlation_id and preferably a trace_id. Propagate through internal RPCs.
- Tracing: instrument spans for http.request, runtime.inference, batch.join, and kernel.execution. Sampling: 100% for errors, 1% for success.
- Logs: structured JSON with fields: timestamp, level, service, correlation_id, trace_id, module, message, and metadata. Avoid PII in logs; redact customer data by default.
Dashboards & Alerts:
- Per-service dashboards in Grafana. Alert definitions live in /dashboards/alerts/*. Thresholds should be tied to SLO burn rates; escalate to oncall when error_rate > 1% for more than 5m or p95 latency > threshold for 10m.

6) Performance Standards
Goal: predictable latency and cost-efficiency.
SLO guidance (examples):
- Public inference API (non-streaming, small responses): p50 < 80ms, p95 < 300ms, error_rate < 0.5%.
- Embeddings API: p50 < 50ms, p95 < 150ms.
- Model load time (cold start): < 60s for large models; for Dedicated pools, < 10s.
Benchmarking:
- Runbench harness required for all model onboarding. Include microbenchmarks (throughput tokens/s), memory footprint, and latency distribution at target sequence lengths (e.g., 128, 512, 1024).
- Baseline hardware profiles: specify expected numbers for A100 and H100. Submit results to benchmarking-and-perf-suite directory.
Optimization controls:
- Default autoscaling policies and safe upper bounds set in infra module. Batching and caching defaults tuned per model class but must be tuned per-customer for Dedicated/Private deployments.

7) Decision Records (ADRs)
Every significant architecture decision must have an ADR. ADRs live in /adrs and follow the template: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Date, Authors.
Example (summary):
- ADR-2025-03: Internal RPC protocol. Decision: use gRPC + protobufs for service-to-service runtime RPCs to optimize binary payloads and streaming inference. Rationale: better flow control and lower CPU overhead vs JSON/HTTP for high-throughput paths. Consequences: invest in cross-language stubs, add proto linting and versioning rules.

8) Ownership and Governance
- Service owners: every service must list an oncall rotation owner and an archival owner in README.
- Reviews: architecture/ADR reviews required for cross-team impact. Use the architecture review board (set of rotating engineers) for high-impact ADR approvals.
- Periodic audits: annually review model catalog and quantization profiles; quarterly review infra modules for drift.

Appendices: Examples & Templates
- OpenAPI snippet, Terraform module header, and model-catalog example included below.
OpenAPI header example:
openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Redwood Inference API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Text generation
      responses:
        '200':
          description: successful generation

Model catalog example (YAML):
- model_id: redwood-7b-v1.2
  architecture: transformer-decoder
  quantization: fp16
  memory_gb: "24"
  expected_throughput_tokens_per_sec: "8000"
  owner: infra-inference

Terraform module header example:
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal/modules.git//gpu-pool?ref=v1.2"
  region = var.region
  desired_capacity = var.desired_capacity
}

Governance & Next steps
- This doc is the baseline. Teams must propose exceptions via ADRs with migration plans and measurable rollback criteria.
- Action: each owning team should verify conformance of their top-10 services to these rules by Q2 2025 and surface gaps to Architecture and EngOps.
